title: Bài thi cuối cấp 6 – Chinh phục IELTS 8.0+
intro:
Bài thi mô phỏng một buổi thi IELTS Academic rút gọn, bao phủ toàn bộ 10 bài của cấp 6. Làm trong điều kiện thật: không từ điển, bấm giờ từng phần, nghe mỗi bài một lần.

PhầnNội dungThời gian gợi ýChấm
1–2. Listening1 bài giảng + 1 thảo luận học thuật, 20 câu~25 phútTự động
3–4. Reading2 bài đọc học thuật, 20 câu40 phútTự động
5. Writing Task 1Biểu đồ cột (số liệu hư cấu), ≥ 150 từ20 phútTự chấm theo rubric + bài mẫu
6. Writing Task 2Đề Opinion, ≥ 250 từ40 phútTự chấm theo rubric + bài mẫu
7. SpeakingPart 1 – 2 – 3, ghi âm~14 phútTự chấm theo rubric + bài mẫu

Đạt cấp: ≥ 70% câu tự chấm (28/40). Tuy nhiên, với mục tiêu 8.0+, hãy nhắm ≥ 35/40 (ước lượng phổ biến: 35–36/40 ở Listening/Reading thật tương đương khoảng band 8.0; quy đổi thật thay đổi theo từng đề). Viết và Nói: tự chấm bằng rubric – nếu có tiêu chí dưới 7.0, hãy quay lại bài tương ứng (bài 1–4 cho ngôn ngữ, bài 5–8 cho ý tưởng, bài 10 cho tự chấm).

sections.intro: Bài giảng về giấc ngủ của thanh thiếu niên và giờ vào học (liên quan bài 7–8, kỹ thuật bài 9). Đọc trước câu hỏi 30 giây, nghe MỘT lần. Câu điền: ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER. Câu 10: chép chính tả một câu trong bài.

lines.t: Good morning. In today's lecture I want to look at a question that sounds trivial but turns out to have significant consequences for education: why do teenagers find it so hard to get up in the morning?
The popular explanation is laziness, or perhaps too much time on phones. Screens certainly play a part, but they are not the root of the problem.

The main cause is biological. During puberty, the body's internal clock, its circadian rhythm, shifts later. The hormone melatonin, which makes us feel sleepy, is released later in the evening in adolescents than in children or adults.
In practical terms, this means that a typical sixteen-year-old may not feel tired until around eleven at night, even if they have been perfectly sensible all evening.
Now, most researchers agree that teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep. If a student falls asleep at eleven and has to get up at six to catch a bus, the arithmetic simply doesn't work.

The result is what's sometimes called chronic sleep debt, and its effects go well beyond tiredness. Poor sleep has been linked to weaker concentration, lower mood and, among teenagers who drive, a higher risk of accidents.
So what can be done? The most widely discussed policy is to start the school day later.

Let me describe one case, which I'll call the Lindale district, because the details have been simplified for teaching purposes. Lindale moved the start of its secondary schools from seven thirty to eight thirty.
Initially, the plan was to delay the start by a full ninety minutes, but this was rejected because of the impact on parents' working hours, so the final change was one hour.
After the change, students reported sleeping on average about forty minutes longer on school nights. Interestingly, they did not simply go to bed later, which is what critics had predicted.

Attendance at the first lesson improved noticeably, and teachers described students as more alert. The effect on exam results was positive but modest, and frankly, it's too early to say whether it will last.

Of course, the policy has costs. The biggest one, in Lindale's case, was not the bus timetable, as many had expected, but after-school sport. Training sessions had to finish later, which meant some teams were practising in the dark during winter.
There were also concerns from families with younger children who relied on older siblings to take them to school.
What lessons can we draw? First, sleep should be treated as a public health issue, not simply a matter of personal discipline.
Second, schedule changes work best when they are combined with education about sleep, for example, encouraging students to keep their phones out of the bedroom.
And finally, any reform needs to be negotiated with the whole community, because the school day shapes the lives of far more people than just the students.
In next week's session, we'll look at how sleep affects memory, so please read chapter four before then.

items.q: 1. The popular explanation for teenagers' late sleep is laziness or too much time on ___.
items.e: “The popular explanation is laziness, or perhaps too much time on phones.” Ngay sau đó giảng viên nói màn hình “not the root of the problem” – đây là quan điểm phổ biến, không phải nguyên nhân chính.

items.q: 2. The hormone that makes us feel sleepy: ___.
items.e: “The hormone melatonin, which makes us feel sleepy, is released later…”. Từ chuyên ngành – chú ý chính tả m-e-l-a-t-o-n-i-n.

items.q: 3. According to the lecturer, what is the MAIN cause of teenagers going to sleep late?
o: A biological shift in the body clock
items.e: “The main cause is biological… the body's internal clock… shifts later.” A và B là “popular explanation” bị bác bỏ ngay câu trước (bẫy kiểu bài 9: ý kiến phổ biến ≠ ý kiến người nói).

items.q: 4. Most researchers agree that teenagers need between eight and ___ hours of sleep.
items.e: “between eight and ten hours of sleep”. Điền số dạng chữ hoặc chữ số đều được.

items.q: 5. The long-term effect of too little sleep is called chronic sleep ___.
items.e: “what's sometimes called chronic sleep debt” = nợ ngủ mạn tính. Âm /b/ trong debt câm: /det/.

items.q: 6. By how much did Lindale finally delay the start of the school day?
items.e: Bẫy đổi kế hoạch: “Initially, the plan was to delay the start by a full ninety minutes, but this was rejected… so the final change was one hour.” (7:30 → 8:30).

items.q: 7. After the change, students slept about ___ minutes longer on school nights.
items.e: “about forty minutes longer on school nights”. Đừng nhầm với 90 (kế hoạch ban đầu) hay 60 (mức lùi giờ thực tế).

items.q: 8. What does the lecturer say about exam results?
o: They improved slightly, but the effect may not last.
They fell because students went to bed later.
items.e: “positive but modest… too early to say whether it will last” = tăng nhẹ, chưa chắc bền. C sai: học sinh KHÔNG đi ngủ muộn hơn như dự đoán của người phản đối.

items.q: 9. What was the biggest cost of the policy in Lindale?
items.e: “The biggest one… was not the bus timetable, as many had expected, but after-school sport.” Cấu trúc “not X but Y” – đáp án luôn nằm ở Y.

items.say: Sleep should be treated as a public health issue, not simply a matter of personal discipline.
items.a: Sleep should be treated as a public health issue, not simply a matter of personal discipline.
items.e: Câu 10. Chú ý bị động “should be treated as”, cụm “a public health issue”, “a matter of personal discipline”.

sections.h: Phần 2 – Listening: Thảo luận dự án nghiên cứu (câu 11–20)
sections.intro: Hai sinh viên Linh và Sam trao đổi với giảng viên hướng dẫn về dự án “Người trẻ kiểm chứng tin tức trên mạng như thế nào” (liên quan bài 6, kỹ thuật bài 9). Chú ý các lần ĐỔI Ý. Câu điền: ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER.

lines.t: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your research project on how young people check news online. How's it going?
Quite well, I think. We've finished the literature review, and we've designed our survey. We were originally going to ask two hundred students, but we've cut that down to a hundred and twenty.
Why's that?
Mainly time. Each survey takes about fifteen minutes, and we also want to do follow-up interviews, so a smaller sample seemed more realistic.
That's sensible. A hundred and twenty is fine for a project of this size, provided you're clear about the limitations. How are you recruiting people?

At first we thought about putting posters up around campus, but we'd mostly get students from our own faculty. So instead we're asking lecturers in five different departments to share the link in their online classes.
Good, that should give you a broader mix. And what exactly are you measuring?
We show participants six headlines, three genuine and three invented, and ask them to rate how believable each one is. Then we ask what, if anything, they'd do to check it.
Interesting. Have you piloted it?

Yes, with eight friends. And that was really useful, because we found that the word verify confused some people. They thought it meant checking the spelling of the article. So we've replaced it with check whether it's true.
Ah, that's a classic pilot finding. What did the pilot suggest about people's habits?
The most common strategy was reading the comments under the post, which surprised us. We'd expected people to search for the story on other news sites, but only two did that.

Hmm. Reading the comments isn't necessarily a bad strategy, but it's risky, because comments can be just as unreliable as the original post. That could be a really interesting angle for your discussion section.
That's what we thought. We're also wondering whether to include a question about age, or whether that's pointless since everyone is a student.
I'd ask about year of study rather than age. First-year and final-year students might behave quite differently, and that's more meaningful in your context.
Okay. And the deadline for the draft is still the twentieth?
Actually, it's been moved to the twenty-seventh, because of the public holiday. But I'd like to see your interview questions by next Friday, so we can sort out any problems early.
Great, thank you. That gives us a bit more breathing space.

items.q: 11. Final number of students the survey will be sent to: ___.
items.e: “We were originally going to ask two hundred students, but we've cut that down to a hundred and twenty.” Bẫy kinh điển: con số đầu tiên (200) đã bị thay.

items.q: 12. Why did the students reduce the size of their sample?
o: They did not have enough time.
items.e: “Mainly time. Each survey takes about fifteen minutes, and we also want to do follow-up interviews.” Giảng viên chỉ đồng ý sau đó, không phải người yêu cầu (A).

items.q: 13. How are the students recruiting participants?
items.e: Đổi ý: “At first we thought about putting posters up… So instead we're asking lecturers in five different departments.” Poster là phương án đã bị loại; “their own faculty only” chính là lý do loại poster (we'd mostly get students from our own faculty).

items.q: 14. Number of headlines shown to each participant: ___.
items.e: “We show participants six headlines, three genuine and three invented” – tổng là 6, không phải 3.

items.q: 15. What problem did the pilot study reveal?
o: The headlines were too easy to judge.
items.e: “the word verify confused some people. They thought it meant checking the spelling.” Các phương án khác không được nhắc đến.

items.q: 16. 'Verify' has been replaced with 'check whether it's ___'.
items.e: “So we've replaced it with check whether it's true.”

items.q: 17. In the pilot, what was the most common way of checking a story?
o: Reading the comments under the post
items.e: “The most common strategy was reading the comments under the post… We'd expected people to search for the story on other news sites, but only two did that.” A là điều họ KỲ VỌNG, không phải điều xảy ra.

items.q: 18. What is the tutor's view of reading comments as a checking strategy?
o: It is the most reliable method available.
It should be removed from the study.
It is risky because comments may be unreliable too.
It is used mainly by first-year students.
items.e: “isn't necessarily a bad strategy, but it's risky, because comments can be just as unreliable as the original post.” Ông còn gợi ý đưa nó vào phần thảo luận – ngược với “removed from the study”.

items.q: 19. The tutor suggests asking about year of ___ instead of age.
items.e: “I'd ask about year of study rather than age.” “rather than” → “instead of” (paraphrase).

items.q: 20. When is the draft now due?
o: At the end of next month
items.e: “Actually, it's been moved to the twenty-seventh.” Bẫy: 20th là hạn cũ; next Friday là hạn nộp CÂU HỎI PHỎNG VẤN, không phải bản nháp.

sections.intro: Bài đọc về chợ đêm và kinh tế phi chính thức ở đô thị Đông Nam Á (liên quan bài 7–8). Gợi ý thời gian: 20 phút.

read.title: The Return of the Night Market
read.text:
A In many Southeast Asian cities, the night market is as much a part of the urban landscape as the office tower. From late afternoon, car parks, side streets and empty lots are transformed into corridors of food stalls, clothing racks and phone-accessory sellers, only to be dismantled again before dawn. For much of the late twentieth century, however, urban planners regarded such markets with suspicion. Informal trading was associated with congestion, poor hygiene and lost tax revenue, and in several cities it was pushed to the margins or banned outright in the name of modernisation.

B That attitude has shifted considerably. Part of the reason is economic. Studies of informal economies across the region suggest that street trading provides a livelihood for very large numbers of people, many of whom lack the qualifications or capital to enter formal employment. For recent migrants from the countryside, in particular, a market stall often represents the first rung on the urban economic ladder. Removing such opportunities without providing alternatives, critics argue, does not eliminate poverty; it merely relocates it.

C A second reason concerns the way cities are experienced. Researchers who study public space have noted that night markets do something that shopping malls rarely achieve: they draw a socially mixed crowd into the same space at the same time. Office workers, students, families and tourists jostle along the same narrow aisles, and the low cost of entry – there is no door, no dress code and no obligation to buy – makes the market unusually inclusive. In cities where land prices have pushed many residents into small apartments, these markets also function as an extension of the home: a place to eat, socialise and escape the heat of the day.

D None of this means that the problems identified by earlier planners were imaginary. Markets that grow without any oversight can block emergency access, generate considerable waste and create tensions with residents who have to live alongside the noise. The more recent approach, adopted in a number of cities, has therefore been to regulate rather than remove. Typically, this involves designating specific sites and hours, issuing licences to vendors, and providing basic infrastructure such as lighting, water points and waste collection. In return, vendors pay a modest fee and agree to meet hygiene standards.

E The results of this approach have been mixed. Where it has worked well, licensing has given vendors a degree of security they previously lacked: a trader with a licence is less vulnerable to arbitrary fines and can plan for the future. Some city authorities have also found that well-managed markets attract tourists and generate revenue for surrounding businesses. Elsewhere, however, licence fees have been set too high for the poorest traders, who have simply continued to operate illegally on nearby streets, undermining the whole scheme. In a few cases, popular markets have been 'upgraded' into covered food halls with higher rents, so that the original vendors have gradually been replaced by chain outlets.

F The lesson, according to many urban researchers, is that the informal economy cannot be managed effectively without the participation of the people who depend on it. Schemes designed in consultation with vendors' associations tend to set fees that traders can afford and to choose locations where customers actually go. The night market, in other words, is not an obstacle to the modern city but one of its most adaptable institutions, provided that policy works with its logic rather than against it.

items.q: 21. Choose the correct heading for paragraph B.
o: A livelihood for those excluded from formal work
A space that brings different people together
The rise of the shopping mall
A plan to ban all street trading
items.e: Đoạn B: street trading “provides a livelihood for… people… [who] lack the qualifications or capital to enter formal employment”. “Why markets were once unwelcome” là nội dung đoạn A (bẫy: đoạn B mở bằng “That attitude has shifted” – nhắc lại A nhưng ý chính là kinh tế).

items.q: 22. Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
o: A livelihood for those excluded from formal work
A space that brings different people together
The rise of the shopping mall
A plan to ban all street trading
items.e: “they draw a socially mixed crowd into the same space at the same time… unusually inclusive”. Shopping malls chỉ được nhắc để so sánh – không phải ý chính (bẫy “từ trùng”).

items.q: 23. Choose the correct heading for paragraph E.
o: A livelihood for those excluded from formal work
A space that brings different people together
The rise of the shopping mall
A plan to ban all street trading
items.e: “The results of this approach have been mixed. Where it has worked well… Elsewhere, however…” = thành công và thất bại của việc quản lý bằng giấy phép.

items.q: 24. TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN: In the late twentieth century, some cities banned informal trading completely.
items.e: Đoạn A: “in several cities it was pushed to the margins or banned outright” – banned outright = cấm hoàn toàn.

items.q: 25. TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN: Most night-market vendors are recent migrants from the countryside.
items.e: Đoạn B chỉ nói với người mới nhập cư “in particular”, quầy hàng thường là nấc thang đầu tiên; bài không nói họ chiếm đa số người bán → NOT GIVEN. Bẫy khái quát quá mức (bài 1).

items.q: 26. TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN: Visitors to night markets are expected to buy something.
items.e: Đoạn C: “no obligation to buy” → mâu thuẫn trực tiếp → FALSE.

items.q: 27. TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN: In some places, licence fees were too expensive for the poorest traders.
items.e: Đoạn E: “licence fees have been set too high for the poorest traders” – “Elsewhere” = “in some places”.

items.q: 28. Under the newer approach, cities designate sites and hours, issue licences and provide basic ___ such as lighting and water points. (ONE WORD)
items.e: Đoạn D: “providing basic infrastructure such as lighting, water points and waste collection”.

items.q: 29. In return, vendors pay a modest fee and agree to meet ___. (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS)
items.e: Đoạn D: “vendors pay a modest fee and agree to meet hygiene standards”. Câu hỏi giữ nguyên cấu trúc – cẩn thận chép đủ 2 từ.

items.q: 30. What does the writer suggest about turning markets into covered food halls?
o: It has generally helped the original vendors.
It is the approach most researchers recommend.
It has reduced the number of tourists.
It can lead to the original vendors being replaced.
items.e: Đoạn E: “the original vendors have gradually been replaced by chain outlets”. Dấu nháy quanh ‘upgraded’ cho thấy thái độ hoài nghi của tác giả – kỹ năng đọc thái độ ở band 8.

sections.intro: Bài đọc về canh tác lúa và phát thải khí mê-tan (liên quan bài 5; câu 40 kiểm tra từ vựng chính xác của bài 2). Gợi ý thời gian: 20 phút.

read.title: Can Rice Farming Cut Its Carbon?
read.text:
A Rice feeds more than half of the world's population, but its cultivation comes with a hidden environmental cost. When paddy fields are kept continuously flooded, the water cuts off the supply of oxygen to the soil. In these conditions, microbes that thrive without oxygen break down organic matter and release methane, a greenhouse gas that is far more potent than carbon dioxide over the short term. As a result, flooded rice fields are one of the largest agricultural sources of methane worldwide.

B Farmers flood their fields for good reasons. Standing water suppresses weeds, helps to regulate soil temperature and, in many traditional systems, requires little decision-making once the field has been filled. In deltas such as the Mekong, where fresh water has historically been plentiful, continuous flooding has been the norm for generations. Changing this practice therefore involves not just new techniques but a shift in deeply rooted habits.

C One technique that has attracted considerable attention is known as alternate wetting and drying, or AWD. Instead of keeping the field permanently flooded, the farmer allows the water level to fall below the surface of the soil for several days before irrigating again. A simple tool makes this possible: a plastic tube, perforated with holes and pushed into the soil, through which the farmer can see the water level underground. When the water drops to around fifteen centimetres below the surface, it is time to re-flood the field.

D The benefits can be substantial. Because the soil is periodically exposed to air, methane-producing microbes are less active, and field trials in several Asian countries have reported reductions in methane emissions of roughly a third or more. AWD also saves water, which matters increasingly in regions affected by drought or by saltwater intrusion, and it can reduce costs for farmers who irrigate with diesel pumps. Importantly, when the technique is applied correctly, yields are generally maintained.

E The technique is not without drawbacks, however. Drying the soil encourages the release of another greenhouse gas, nitrous oxide, although most studies suggest that the overall climate benefit remains positive. More practically, AWD requires fields that are reasonably level and irrigation that farmers can control. Where water is supplied to a whole area at once through shared canals, an individual farmer may be unable to drain or flood a field at the right time. In such cases, coordination between neighbouring farmers, or investment in local infrastructure, becomes essential.

F For these reasons, researchers increasingly argue that the spread of AWD depends less on the technique itself than on the incentives surrounding it. Farmers who pay for pumped water have an obvious motive to adopt it; those who receive water free of charge have little reason to change. Some programmes have experimented with payments linked to verified emission reductions, while others have combined AWD with training in fertiliser use, so that farmers see a direct saving in costs. Whether such schemes can be scaled up to millions of smallholdings remains an open question, but the potential prize – lower emissions from one of the world's most important crops – is considerable.

items.q: 31. Which paragraph explains why farmers have traditionally kept their fields flooded?
items.e: Đoạn B: “Farmers flood their fields for good reasons. Standing water suppresses weeds, helps to regulate soil temperature…”.

items.q: 32. Which paragraph describes a tool used to monitor the water level?
items.e: Đoạn C: “a plastic tube, perforated with holes… through which the farmer can see the water level underground”.

items.q: 33. TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN: Over the short term, methane has a stronger warming effect than carbon dioxide.
items.e: Đoạn A: “far more potent than carbon dioxide over the short term” – potent = mạnh (về hiệu ứng nhà kính).

items.q: 34. TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN: AWD usually causes a significant fall in rice yields.
items.e: Đoạn D: “when the technique is applied correctly, yields are generally maintained” → mâu thuẫn → FALSE.

items.q: 35. TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN: Most farmers in the Mekong Delta have already adopted AWD.
items.e: Mekong chỉ được nhắc như ví dụ về tập quán ngập nước liên tục; bài không nói tỉ lệ nông dân áp dụng AWD → NOT GIVEN.

items.q: 36. The field should be flooded again when the water is about ___ centimetres below the surface. (A NUMBER)
items.e: Đoạn C: “When the water drops to around fifteen centimetres below the surface, it is time to re-flood the field.”

items.q: 37. AWD may increase emissions of ___, another greenhouse gas. (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS)
items.e: Đoạn E: “Drying the soil encourages the release of another greenhouse gas, nitrous oxide”.

items.q: 38. According to paragraph E, AWD is difficult to use when…
o: water is supplied to a whole area through shared canals.
items.e: “Where water is supplied to a whole area at once through shared canals, an individual farmer may be unable to drain or flood a field at the right time.” C là trường hợp AWD có LỢI (đoạn D).

items.q: 39. Why are farmers who receive free water less likely to adopt AWD?
o: They gain no direct saving from using less water.
Their fields are usually too uneven.
They are not allowed to drain their fields.
items.e: Đoạn F: người trả tiền bơm nước “have an obvious motive”; người được nước miễn phí “have little reason to change” – vì tiết kiệm nước không giúp họ bớt chi phí. Đây là câu suy luận (inference) kiểu band 8.

items.q: 40. In paragraph B, the phrase “deeply rooted habits” is closest in meaning to…
items.e: deeply rooted = deeply entrenched (bài 2) = ăn sâu bám rễ, đã thành nếp. Không mang nghĩa “có hại” (C) – bài thậm chí nói nông dân ngập ruộng “for good reasons”.

sections.intro: Viết ít nhất 150 từ. Số liệu hư cấu. Ngôn ngữ số liệu xem bài 10; overview và độ chính xác xem bài 1.

write.task:
The chart below shows the percentage of household waste that was sent to landfill, recycled, composted and incinerated in the city of Riverton in 2005, 2015 and 2025.
Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
(Riverton và số liệu là hư cấu, chỉ dùng để luyện tập.)

chart.title: Household waste treatment in Riverton, 2005–2025 (fictional data)

write.model:
The bar chart compares the proportions of household waste in the city of Riverton that were sent to landfill, recycled, composted and incinerated in 2005, 2015 and 2025.

Overall, the city shifted decisively away from landfill over the twenty-year period, with recycling overtaking it to become the most common method by 2025. All three alternatives to landfill expanded their share, although composting and incineration remained comparatively minor.

In 2005, landfill accounted for the vast majority of household waste, at 72%, while recycling, incineration and composting together made up just over a quarter (12%, 10% and 6% respectively). Over the following decade, the share sent to landfill fell to 51%, and recycling rose substantially to 21%, with incineration and composting reaching 17% and 11%.

By 2025, the picture had changed fundamentally. Landfill's share had dropped to 28%, less than half of its 2005 level, whereas recycling had climbed to 34%, nearly three times its original figure. Composting also grew markedly, more than tripling from 6% to 19%, and thus matched the share of incineration, which had almost doubled since 2005.
rubric: Task Achievement: có câu giới thiệu paraphrase đề (không chép nguyên văn) và một OVERVIEW riêng nêu 2 xu hướng lớn nhất (landfill giảm mạnh; recycling vượt lên dẫn đầu) – không chứa số liệu chi tiết
Mọi số liệu trích dẫn khớp TUYỆT ĐỐI với biểu đồ; các phép so sánh đúng toán (34 gần gấp 3 lần 12; 28 < một nửa của 72; 6 → 19 là hơn gấp ba)
Coherence: nhóm số liệu theo mốc thời gian hoặc theo phương pháp một cách nhất quán; mỗi đoạn thân bài có trọng tâm rõ
Lexical: ngôn ngữ số liệu chính xác, đa dạng (account for, respectively, overtake, less than half, more than triple) – không lặp “increase/decrease”
Grammar: thì quá khứ đơn/quá khứ hoàn thành đúng mốc (By 2025… had dropped); ≥ 2/3 số câu sạch lỗi
Không đưa ý kiến cá nhân hay giải thích nguyên nhân; ≥ 150 từ (bài mẫu ≈ 190 từ)

sections.intro: Viết ít nhất 250 từ. Vận dụng: lập trường đúng mức (bài 1), collocation chính xác (bài 2), ngữ pháp đa dạng có chức năng (bài 3), ngân hàng ý tưởng (bài 5–8).

write.task:
Some people argue that international tourism does more harm than good to the places that tourists visit.
To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
write.model:
Few industries divide opinion as sharply as international tourism. For some, it is a lifeline that sustains millions of jobs; for others, it is a force that erodes the very places it claims to celebrate. In my view, tourism is not inherently harmful, but in many popular destinations its costs currently outweigh its benefits, largely because those costs are borne by local residents while much of the profit flows elsewhere.

The case against tourism is strongest in places that receive far more visitors than they were designed for. In historic towns and on small islands, mass tourism places enormous strain on water supplies, waste systems and housing. When apartments are converted into short-term rentals, rents rise and long-standing residents are gradually priced out, so that the community which gave the place its character slowly disappears. Environmental damage follows a similar pattern: coral reefs, beaches and mountain trails can be degraded within a few years by visitor numbers that local authorities are simply unable to manage.

Nevertheless, it would be a mistake to conclude that tourism is harmful by nature. In regions with few alternative industries, it can provide stable employment, particularly for young people and women, and it gives communities a financial incentive to preserve traditional crafts and natural landscapes rather than replace them with factories. Homestay programmes in mountainous areas, for instance, have allowed families to earn a living from hosting visitors while retaining ownership of their land.

What determines whether tourism helps or harms, therefore, is not the presence of visitors but the way the industry is managed. Destinations that cap visitor numbers, levy tourist taxes and reinvest the revenue in local infrastructure tend to retain the benefits while limiting the damage. Where such measures are absent, the harm is often severe and, in the case of fragile ecosystems, irreversible.

In conclusion, I agree that international tourism currently does more harm than good in many destinations, but only because it is so often poorly regulated. Managed with the interests of residents at its centre, it has the potential to be a genuine force for good.
rubric: Task Response: trả lời đúng câu hỏi “to what extent” – lập trường rõ, có mức độ (đồng ý một phần, có điều kiện) và NHẤT QUÁN từ mở bài đến kết bài
Mỗi đoạn thân bài một ý trung tâm, phát triển sâu: cơ chế (vì sao) + ví dụ cụ thể; không liệt kê nhiều lý do nông
Coherence & Cohesion: liên kết bằng quy chiếu và danh từ khái quát (those costs, such measures, this pattern) thay vì chuỗi Firstly/Moreover; phân đoạn hợp lý
Lexical Resource: collocation chính xác (place strain on, priced out, levy taxes, retain benefits), không lặp từ khoá máy móc, không có thành ngữ văn nói
Grammatical Range & Accuracy: đa dạng có chức năng (bị động, mệnh đề quan hệ, câu chẻ “What determines… is…”, phân từ); ≥ 2/3 số câu hoàn toàn sạch lỗi
≥ 250 từ (bài mẫu ≈ 370 từ); không khái quát tuyệt đối (all, always, everyone) khi chưa chứng minh

sections.intro: Ghi âm cả ba phần liên tục như thi thật (Part 2: 1 phút chuẩn bị, nói đến 2 phút). Sau đó nghe lại, chép lời 1 câu trả lời Part 3 và tự chấm theo rubric (bài 4 và bài 10).

tasks.p: Part 1: Do you enjoy visiting museums? Why or why not?
tasks.model: I do, although I'll admit I don't go as often as I'd like. What I enjoy most are small, specialised museums rather than the big national ones, because each exhibit tends to tell a personal story instead of just listing dates. I find I remember far more from an afternoon in a place like that than from a whole day in a huge gallery.

tasks.p: Part 1: How do you usually find out about the news?
tasks.model: Mostly through my phone, to be honest – usually headlines on a news app while I'm having breakfast. That said, I've become a lot more careful over the past couple of years. If a story seems surprising, I'll check whether a reputable outlet is reporting it before I share it with anyone.

tasks.p: Part 2: Describe a place in your city that has changed a lot in recent years. You should say: where it is; what it used to be like; how it has changed; and explain how you feel about these changes.
tasks.model: I'd like to talk about the area around a small lake near where I grew up, on the western side of Hanoi. When I was a child, it was fairly run-down, to be honest. The lake itself was quite polluted, there was rubbish along the banks, and the only real activity was a wet market in the mornings, where my grandmother used to buy vegetables. Over the last ten years or so, it's been transformed. The local authorities cleaned up the water and built a walking path all the way round, with benches and trees. A lot of the old shophouses have been turned into cafés and small boutiques, and on weekend evenings the main road is closed to traffic, so families come out to walk, children ride their bikes and street performers set up along the path. How do I feel about it? Mostly positive, I have to say. It's far more pleasant to spend time there now, and it's given the neighbourhood a sense of community that it didn't really have before. Having said that, the changes have come at a cost. Rents have gone up considerably, and several of the families who used to run the market stalls have moved further out because they couldn't afford to stay. The market itself is much smaller now. So my feelings are a bit mixed: I love what the area has become, but I can't help feeling that some of the people who made it what it was have been left behind.

tasks.p: Part 3: Should cities preserve old buildings or replace them with modern ones?
tasks.model: I don't think it has to be one or the other. Some old buildings clearly deserve protection – the ones with genuine historical or architectural value – because once they're gone, they're gone for good. But it would be unrealistic to preserve everything. Cities are growing fast, people need housing, and some older buildings are frankly unsafe or impossible to adapt. What I'd like to see more of is what's sometimes called adaptive reuse: keeping the structure of an old building but giving it a new function, say turning a disused factory into a library or an arts centre. That way you keep the character of the street while still meeting modern needs. The worst outcome, in my view, is when historic districts are demolished and replaced with generic towers that could be anywhere in the world.

tasks.p: Part 3: How might tourism change over the next twenty years?
tasks.model: Well, it's hard to predict with any certainty, but I suspect we'll see far more control over visitor numbers. Some popular destinations are already introducing booking systems or entry fees, and I imagine that will become the norm rather than the exception. There'll probably also be a shift towards slower, longer trips, partly because of the environmental cost of flying and partly because people seem increasingly interested in experiencing everyday life somewhere rather than ticking off famous sights. Technology will play a role too – virtual tours might satisfy some people's curiosity about places they'll never actually visit. That said, I don't think anything will fully replace the experience of being somewhere in person, so I doubt demand for travel will fall; it'll just be managed more carefully.

rubric: Fluency & Coherence: nói liền mạch; nếu ngập ngừng là để nghĩ ý chứ không phải tìm từ; Part 3 có cấu trúc (lập trường → lý do → ví dụ → nhượng bộ → kết) bằng discourse markers tự nhiên
Lexical Resource: dùng từ chính xác để diễn đạt sắc thái (run-down, adaptive reuse, priced out); thành ngữ tối đa 1–2 mỗi câu trả lời, đúng chỗ, không sáo
Grammatical Range & Accuracy: phối hợp tự nhiên các thì (hiện tại hoàn thành cho thay đổi, will/might cho dự đoán), câu phức, câu chẻ; phần lớn câu không lỗi khi chép lại
Pronunciation: âm cuối rõ (-s, -ed), trọng âm từ đúng, trọng âm đối lập khi so sánh, ngữ điệu xuống ở câu khẳng định, nối âm và dạng yếu tự nhiên
Part 2 nói đủ khoảng 2 phút, bao đủ 4 gợi ý, phần “explain how you feel” được phát triển nhất
Tự chấm: nghe lại bản ghi, đếm số lần ngập ngừng vì tìm từ và số lỗi trong 1 câu trả lời Part 3 đã chép; ≤ 2 lỗi nhỏ/100 từ là dấu hiệu tốt cho band 8
